# A fixed-half-mass moment centroid works for three interval fibers

This is a proved selector theorem for n=d=1 and at most three consecutive
positive-length fibers. It is not a proof of OC in higher dimension or for
arbitrarily many fibers. Its new feature relative to the earlier
`candidate 5939c45de14c2bb5` is the mass range
`t >= M/2`, rather than the failed prescribed mass `D_j/2`.

## 1. Definitions and existence

Let C be a planar convex body whose positive-length integer fibers are
among the bases -1,0,1, and let mu be their length measure, of total mass M.
A weighted median base j is an integer base such that both closed integer
half-lines containing j have mass at least M/2. Such a j exists.

For a prescribed mass t, let B_t(j) be the interval of continuous
barycenters of measures sigma <= mu satisfying

    sigma(S)=t,       integral z d sigma=t j.

The feasible set is weak-star compact in the densities 0<=f<=1, so B_t(j)
is compact and convex whenever nonempty. Its points belong to C_j by
convexity. The theorem below only uses feasible t >= M/2. In particular
t=M/2 is feasible: the general inequality T_max(j)>=D_j>=M/2 is proved in
`candidate b4c3b9c6a52059d2`, Section 1.
For three fibers feasibility also follows from the scalar constraints
in Section 3 below.

**Theorem.** For every weighted median base j and every feasible t>=M/2,
the midpoint y of B_t(j) satisfies

    mu(H) >= M/4

for every closed ambient halfspace H containing (j,y).

## 2. Endpoint medians and normalizations

If j is the least or greatest positive-mass base, the zero base-moment
condition forces sigma to lie entirely in that one fiber. The possible
mass-t interval barycenters form an interval concentric with that fiber.
Consequently y is the fiber midpoint. Every ambient halfspace containing
(j,y) retains at least half of that fiber, or the whole fiber if its
normal has zero continuous component. Its length is at least M/2 by the
median condition, proving the claim.

It remains to treat j=0 with a positive-length middle interval. Scale the
continuous coordinate so that this interval is [-1/2,1/2]. A shear
x -> x-k z makes the two endpoint interval centers equal; it preserves
integer fibers, all lengths, the base-balance constraint, and the whole
ambient halfspace family. Write the normalized fibers as

    I_-=[s-a/2,s+a/2],
    I_0=[-1/2,1/2],
    I_+=[s-c/2,s+c/2].

Set r=a+c and m=min(a,c). Convexity gives midpoint interval inclusion,
and hence

    0 <= r <= 2,       |s| <= (2-r)/4.                 (1)

The weighted median condition is equivalent to

    |a-c| <= 1.                                        (2)

The normalized total mass is M=1+r. Reflecting x if needed, assume s>=0.
Zero endpoint lengths are allowed; they carry no length measure.

## 3. Exact support optimization and elementary centroid bounds

Base balance requires equal endpoint selected masses, say ell each.
The middle selected mass is t-2 ell. Thus

    max(0,(t-1)/2) <= ell <= min(a,c,t/2).              (3)

For an interval of length w and center g, the possible first moments
of dominated submeasures of mass v are precisely

    [v g-v(w-v)/2, v g+v(w-v)/2].                      (4)

The endpoints are attained by bottom and top subintervals. The upper
bound follows by the threshold exchange identity: if J is the top
subinterval with threshold b and f is any competing density, then
integral (x-b)(1_J-f) >= 0, while their equal masses cancel b.
The lower bound follows by reflection. Convex interpolation fills the
whole interval of moments.

For fixed ell, sum the three moment intervals. Their center is 2s ell;
write their half-width as Q(ell). It is unnecessary to expand its
quadratic expression. The upper and lower endpoints of B_t(0) are

    U(s)=t^(-1) max_ell [Q(ell)+2s ell],
    L(s)=-t^(-1) max_ell [Q(ell)-2s ell],              (5)

where ell ranges over the same compact interval (3). Put
F(v)=max_ell[Q(ell)+v ell]. Then

    y=(F(2s)-F(-2s))/(2t).

Every ell in (3) lies in [0,min(m,t/2)]. Comparing the two maximization
problems pointwise proves

    0 <= y <= min(s, 2sm/t).

Using t >= (1+r)/2 and (1) therefore gives the bounds

    0 <= y <= s,
    y <= m(2-r)/(1+r).                               (6)

These statements do not assume differentiability or uniqueness of a
support optimizer.

## 4. Exact oblique halfspace optimization

A closed halfspace with nonzero continuous normal can be tightened to
have its boundary through (0,y), without increasing its measure. Its
fiber thresholds have the form y+v z. In the lower orientation, after
allowing all real v, the two endpoint contributions have infimum

    min(m, [2(y-s)+r/2]_+).                           (7)

For completeness, for arbitrary lengths a,c and a fixed sum T of the
two cut lengths before clipping,

    inf_w [clamp(w,0,a)+clamp(T-w,0,c)]
      =min(min(a,c), max(T,0)).

The right side is a lower bound: if either clipped term is saturated,
the sum is at least min(a,c); if neither is saturated, their sum is at
least max(T,0). The lower bound is attained by taking w to an appropriate
endpoint breakpoint, or far enough toward either infinity. This proves
(7). Applying the same identity to upper tails gives the two exact
unnormalized cap infima

    D_low =1/2+y+min(m,[r/2-2s+2y]_+),
    D_up  =1/2-y+min(m,[r/2+2s-2y]_+).                (8)

Since 0<=y<=s and r/2>=m, the upper expression simplifies to

    D_up=1/2-y+m.                                    (9)

Zero-continuous-normal halfspaces have mass at least M/2 by the weighted
median condition, and therefore already exceed the required M/4.

## 5. Both cap bounds

First consider D_low. If r<=1, its middle contribution alone is
1/2+y >= (1+r)/4. Suppose r>=1. By (1),

    r/2-2s+2y >= r-1+2y >= 0.

If the minimum in (8) is m, then

    D_low >= 1/2+m >= (1+r)/4,

where the last inequality follows from |a-c|=r-2m<=1.
If the minimum is the other term, then

    D_low=1/2+r/2-2s+3y
          >=r-1/2
          >=(1+r)/4,

because s<=(2-r)/4, y>=0, and r>=1. Thus all lower caps pass.

By (6), the upper-cap claim follows from

    m(2-r)/(1+r) <= (1+4m-r)/4.                      (10)

After multiplying by 4(1+r), (10) is equivalent to

    1-r^2+4m(2r-1) >= 0.                            (11)

If 0<=r<=1/2, use m<=r/2 and 2r-1<=0 to bound the left side below by
1-2r+3r^2>0. If 1/2<=r<=1, use m>=0 to bound it below by 1-r^2>=0.
If 1<=r<=2, (2) gives m>=(r-1)/2, and the left side is at least

    1-r^2+2(r-1)(2r-1)=3(r-1)^2>=0.

This proves (10); equations (6) and (9) now imply
D_up>=1/2+m-(1+4m-r)/4=(1+r)/4. All closed halfspaces are covered.
Undoing the shear, reflection, and continuous scaling proves the theorem.

## 6. Scope and the next precise test

The theorem supplies an exact positive result for the fixed choice t=M/2
that survived the numerical screen in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/test-fixed-halfmass-moment-selector-density-adversary.py`. The computation
is not used anywhere in the proof.

The proof uses the common endpoint selected mass forced by three-base
balance and the exact clipped two-interval identity. Four or more bases
have additional independent mass transfers, so neither step extends by
notation alone. For n>1 the proposed mass is M/2^n rather than M/2; the
complement symmetry and the threshold t>=M/2 disappear. For d>1 the moment
body has a genuine volume centroid rather than the midpoint of an
interval. Those extensions remain unproved and are not implicit claims.
